items.prompt: Try it: White's knight can take the black rook or the black pawn. Nothing guards either one. Take the one you would rather win.

claims.statement: The knight wins the rook and gives nothing back.
No black piece guards the rook.
Taking the pawn instead is clearly worse than taking the rook.

hints: Both black pieces are loose, so this is only a question of which prize is bigger.
One of the two pieces is a rook. A pawn is the smallest piece.
The rook is on e6, an L-jump from the knight.
items.explain: The knight can reach the rook on e6 or the pawn on f5. Neither is guarded, so either capture is safe, but the rook is the bigger prize: players count it as 5 points and a pawn as 1.

feedback_by_move.d4f5: Taking the pawn is safe, but it wins only 1 point. The rook stays on the board and is worth 5.

items.prompt: Tap every white piece that has a counting value of 3.

claims.statement: The knight stands on b1.
The bishop stands on c1.
The rook stands on a1.
The queen stands on d1.

hints: Remember the table: pawn 1, then two kinds of piece share one number.
The knight and the bishop are the two pieces with the same value.
Look at the back row: the knight is next to the rook, the bishop next to the queen.
items.explain: The knight and the bishop are both worth 3 by the counting values. The rook is worth 5, the queen 9 and each pawn 1.

items.prompt: White thinks about taking the rook on d5 with the knight. The bishop on c6 will recapture. After the captures, what has happened to White's points?

claims.statement: The knight takes a rook, the bishop takes the knight: net plus two.
Exactly one black piece guards the rook.

hints: Is the rook guarded? If yes, you will lose the capturing piece too.
Add what you take, then subtract what you lose.
Name what you take, name what comes back, then subtract.
items.explain: The knight takes a rook (5 points in). The bishop takes the knight (3 points out). Five minus three is plus two, so White gains.

items.prompt: White thinks about taking the rook on d5 with the pawn. The queen on d8 will recapture. After the captures, what has happened to White's points?

claims.statement: The pawn takes a rook, the queen takes the pawn: net plus four.
Exactly one black piece guards the rook.

hints: The queen guards the rook, so the pawn will be taken back.
Add what you take, then subtract what you lose.
Name what you take, name what comes back, then subtract.
items.explain: The pawn takes a rook (5 in). The queen takes the pawn (1 out). Five minus one is plus four: a small piece that takes a big one is a good swap even when it is taken back.

items.prompt: White's queen takes the knight on c6. The bishop takes the queen. Then White's rook takes the bishop. By the counting values, what is White's net result?

claims.statement: After all three captures White is 3 points down.
One black piece, the bishop, guards the knight.

hints: Write the captures as a list: what comes in, what goes out.
In: a knight and a bishop. Out: the queen.
Total the pieces you win and the pieces you give up separately, then compare.
items.explain: White takes a knight (3) and later a bishop (3), 6 points in. White gives up the queen, 9 points out. Six minus nine is minus three, even though White won two pieces for one.

items.prompt: White to move. The rook can take a knight that a pawn guards, or a bishop that nothing guards. Which capture is better?

claims.statement: Taking the loose bishop wins 3 points.
Nothing guards the bishop.
Taking the guarded knight loses the rook for a knight.
A pawn guards the knight.

hints: Ask of each target: is it guarded?
One capture is free. The other gives the rook away for a smaller piece.
The free piece is the bishop on a4, along the fourth row.
items.explain: The knight on d6 is guarded by a pawn, so taking it wins 3 and loses the rook (5). The bishop on a4 is guarded by nothing, so taking it wins 3 for free.

feedback_by_move.d4d6: The pawn takes the rook back. You win 3 points and lose 5, so you end 2 down.

items.prompt: Black has far more points: a queen and a rook against White's knight and two pawns. But it is White's move. Find the move that ends the game.

claims.statement: The knight move is checkmate.
The knight can reach f7.

hints: The count is not what matters when the king can be trapped.
Black's king has no free square: look at what stands on every square next to it.
A knight attacks in an L-shape, and no black piece can take it on its new square.
items.explain: The black king on h8 is boxed in by its own rook and two pawns. The knight jumps to f7 and gives check; no black piece can take it, so this is checkmate. The queen and rook are worth 14 points and do nothing.

items.prompt: White thinks about taking the bishop on c5 with the knight. The pawn on b6 will recapture. After the captures, what has happened to White's points?

claims.statement: Knight for bishop is an even swap.
One pawn guards the bishop.

hints: Is the bishop guarded?
Add what you take, then subtract what you lose.
Look up both pieces in the table and compare them.
items.explain: The knight takes a bishop (3 in). The pawn takes the knight (3 out). Three minus three is zero, an even swap.

items.prompt: Black's pawn on d5 is attacked three times by White (knight, rook, rook) and guarded twice by Black (pawn, rook). Every capture is made, cheapest piece first. What is White's net result?

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack d5 directly; the second rook backs up the first.
Two black pieces guard d5.
The full swap leaves White one point down.

hints: List White's attackers from cheapest to dearest, and Black's defenders the same way.
Alternate: White takes, Black retakes, and so on. Keep a running total.
Add what White takes and subtract what White gives up.
items.explain: White takes a pawn (1), the pawn retakes the knight (3 out), White takes a pawn (1), the rook retakes (5 out), White takes the rook (5). In: 1+1+5 = 7. Out: 3+5 = 8. Net: minus one. Three attackers against two guards sounded good, but the first attacker was a knight, so the swap costs a point.

items.prompt: Black's pawn on d5 is attacked by a knight and two rooks and guarded by a pawn and a rook. White is to move. Is it a good idea to start the captures?

claims.statement: The full swap on d5 ends one point down for White.
Two black pieces guard d5.

hints: Count the attackers and the guards of d5 before you touch anything.
Work out the whole sequence, cheapest piece first, and find the final total.
If the total is below zero, you can simply decline to start.
items.explain: The full sequence ends with White one point down, so the sensible choice is to leave the pawn alone and make a useful move instead. A swap you can calculate to a loss is a swap you do not start.

items.prompt: White to move. The queen is attacked by a bishop and can capture three things. Which capture is best?

claims.statement: Nothing guards the knight on h7.
Taking the guarded pawn loses the queen.
Taking the guarded bishop gives the queen for a bishop.

hints: For each capture, ask whether Black can take back, and with what.
Compare what each capture wins with the piece it risks.
One target has no guard at all.
items.explain: The pawn on d5 and the bishop on b5 are both guarded by a pawn, so each capture loses the queen for a small piece. The knight on h7 has no guard, so the queen takes it for free and leaves the attacked square.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the best move.

claims.statement: The rook move is checkmate.

hints: Where is Black's king, and which squares can it use?
Three pawns stand in front of the king. Which rank is it on?
A rook on that rank attacks the king along it.
items.explain: Black's king is shut in by its own pawns, so the rook gives checkmate on the back rank. The queen's extra points never get a chance to matter.

items.prompt: Tap the white piece that has no legal move.

claims.statement: The rook has no legal move.
The rook stands on a1.

hints: Check each white piece in turn: can it move at all?
The rook sits in the corner.
A knight and a pawn stand next to it.
items.explain: The rook on a1 is closed in by its own knight on b1 and pawn on a2, so it cannot move. Its 5 points are real, but for now they do nothing. One move by the knight would free it.
